subject: Communication
title: Power Poses: Myth or Science?
description: A 60-second lesson on Power Poses: Myth or Science?.

hook.text: Amy Cuddy's TED talk said standing like Wonder Woman for two minutes boosts confidence. 70 million views.

buildup.text: Her 2010 study claimed power poses raise testosterone and lower cortisol, changing your hormones.

discovery.text: Replication studies failed to confirm the hormonal changes. The scientific community pushed back hard.

twist.text: But later research found power poses do affect feelings of confidence — even if hormones don't change.

climax.text: The lesson: posture influences self-perception (embodied cognition), even if the original claims were too bold.

punchline.text: Power poses may not change your chemistry. They might change your mind.

quiz.question: What happened when power pose research was replicated?
options: Hormonal changes weren't confirmed, but confidence effects were

details.summary: Amy Cuddy's 2012 TED talk popularized the idea that adopting expansive poses boosts testosterone and confidence. Replication studies challenged the hormonal claims, but evidence for subjective confidence effects remains mixed.
details.whyItMatters: The power pose debate illustrates how popular psychology can outpace evidence and why critical evaluation of body language claims matters.
takeaways: Power poses were claimed to change hormones and confidence
Replication studies failed to confirm hormonal changes
Subjective feelings of confidence may still be influenced

faq.question: Should I still use power poses before presentations?
faq.answer: Adopting expansive postures may help you feel slightly more confident, even if the hormonal claims are unsupported. The risk is low and the placebo-like benefit may be worth it, but do not expect dramatic physiological changes.

faq.question: Why did the power pose study fail to replicate?
faq.answer: The original study had a small sample size and measured many outcomes. Larger replications found no significant hormonal changes. This became a prominent example in psychology's broader replication crisis.
